facts.fact: Freshwater velvet is caused by the parasitic dinoflagellate Piscinoodinium pillulare. Older texts call it Oodinium.
Velvet is caused by Amyloodinium in marine fish and Oodinium in freshwater fish. It is also called gold-dust, rust or coral disease.
Velvet is highly contagious and can kill fish.
The parasite infects 14 species of tropical ornamental fish from many families, as well as carp and crucian carp.
The gills are the main site of infection and damage. Heavy infections fuse the gill lamellae.
Advanced cases die of hypoxia caused by gill necrosis.
Very young and very old fish have high death rates from velvet.
The life cycle has three stages: the trophont feeds on the fish, the tomont is a resting cyst on the bottom, and the dinospores swim free.
A tomont rests on the tank floor and divides into as many as 256 tomites.
Free-swimming dinospores are the only stage that treatment can kill. Tomonts and trophonts resist chemicals.
Cysts resist chemical treatment, so several applications are usually needed. Free-swimming dinospores are the most vulnerable stage.
Dinospores contain chlorophyll, so they can survive without a host while light is available.
Tomonts can stay dormant in the substrate for weeks or months.
At 23–25°C a trophont matures into a detached tomont in 3–4 days, and the tomont divides into dinospores in 50–70 hours.
At 15–17°C, tomont division takes about 11 days.
The full life cycle takes 10–14 days at 22–25°C and is slower at lower temperatures.
Trophonts take about 6 days to mature at 25°C before dropping off.
Under bright light, the fish looks covered in fine gold dust on the head, body and fins.
The infection often starts on the gills, so the fish can be very sick before any skin signs appear.
Flashing, meaning sudden rubbing against objects, is a common sign.
Signs include clamped fins, lethargy and a brown, gold or greenish dusting. Advanced cases show laboured breathing and refusal to eat.
Early infections show a light golden dusting in oblique light. Heavy infestations can look like dense white dusting.
Fish crowd near the surface or filter outlets. With heavy gill infection they breathe fast with flared gill covers.
Skin may show extra mucus, scale loss, pinpoint bleeding and small ulcers.
Velvet can be confused with ich (white spot). Diagnosis uses skin or gill wet mounts that show sac-shaped trophonts of 80–100 µm.
Trophonts stain dark blue with Lugol's iodine, which helps identify them under a microscope.
Affected fish can look rust-coloured with a thick mucus coat.
Shining a flashlight on the fish in a dark room makes the yellow or rust film on the fins, body and gills easier to see.
Sick fish may stay near the surface gasping. Death is usually from suffocation, sometimes with secondary fungal or bacterial infection.
Velvet spreads through contaminated tanks, fish and tools such as nets. Rarely, frozen live foods carry dormant forms.
The parasite is often already present in a tank and breaks out when the fish's immune system is weakened.
A temperature drop of about 15°F within an hour, or water below about 73°F, can trigger an outbreak.
Wild bettas and blackwater fish are especially prone to velvet.
Dinospores may spread between tanks placed close together through aerosol droplets.
Dirty tanks, poor water quality, large temperature swings and rough handling raise the risk.
Change 30–50% of the water and test pH, temperature, chlorine, ammonia, nitrite and nitrate.
Remove activated carbon from the filter so it does not take the medication out of the water.
Isolate the sick fish in clean water, but treat both tanks because the disease spreads easily.
Copper sulphate: 0.15 ppm copper ion as a bath for up to 10 days, repeated if needed.
Copper sulphate dose (mg/L) = total alkalinity (mg/L) ÷ 100. Do not use it if alkalinity is below 50 mg/L.
Homemade chelated copper: mix 2 parts citric acid with 1 part copper sulphate by weight, and dose by the copper sulphate weight only.
Only use copper sulphate if you can test alkalinity, measure tank volume accurately and weigh the chemical. If unsure, do not use it.
Copper binds to the substrate and can leach back into the water, so levels need frequent testing.
The Amyloodinium method of copper sulphate plus citric acid gives 0.15 ppm copper ion. FAO says such marine methods should work for Piscinoodinium with the dose adjusted.
In freshwater below pH 7.0, copper above 0.3 ppm can kill fish such as Puntius gonionotus fry.
BW Aquatics treats wild bettas with Mardel CopperSafe at about 5 ml per 5 gallons, which it calls roughly 1.5–2.0 ppm copper, at 84°F or above for 30 days.
Copper is more toxic in acidic water, so chelated copper is preferred there.
Heat: raising water to 33–34°C has been reported to control infestations.
Heat above 84°F shortens the life cycle. The author says there is no evidence that heat alone kills the parasite.
Raising the temperature speeds the life cycle, but it does not suit all fish and the stress can weaken their immunity.
For tropical tanks, raise the temperature gradually to 29°C over 24 hours to shorten the parasite's life cycle.
Salt bath: 30 g/L sodium chloride for 5–15 minutes, only for species that tolerate it.
Quinine hydrochloride at 30 mg/L, alone or with malachite green as the maker directs.
In a lab study on swordtails, salinomycin in food at 60 or 90 ppm was fed daily for 16 or 19 days.
Aquarium Co-op's anecdotal method uses plain sodium chloride (not marine salt) at 1 cup per 20 gallons, with the tank kept completely dark for 7 days.
Salt is believed to slow the parasite's reproduction in freshwater but cannot wipe out an outbreak on its own.
Drugs added to the water include copper sulfate, methylene blue, formalin, malachite green and acriflavine. Seven days of total darkness can help alongside them.
UV-C only works with a good bulb of at least 36 W near 250 nm and slow flow. Small submersible units and bulbs near 280 nm do not work.
Velvet usually does not respond to broad-spectrum medications.
Copper toxicity: Caridina shrimp are harmed at about 2 µg Cu/L, and 42 µg Cu/L is acutely toxic to Denariusa bandata.
Half of tested Melanotaenia and Ambassis died at 120–200 µg Cu/L, and half of Macrobrachium at 160 µg Cu/L. Snails are also very sensitive.
Copper sulphate can be dangerous to some fish, plants, shrimp and snails.
Anchor catfish are extremely sensitive to salt.
Malachite green should not be used on catfish, loaches or tetras.
Treat continuously for about a week, and longer in cool water.
1) Change 30–50% of the water and test it. 2) Raise the temperature slowly to 29°C over 24 hours. 3) Dim or turn off the lights. 4) Remove carbon. 5) Add aquarium salt.
Keep treating until the fish show no symptoms. Treat both the quarantine tank and the main tank.
Quarantine new fish for 10–14 days before adding them to the main tank.
Quarantine new plants too, avoid sudden temperature changes, and float the bag for about 15 minutes before releasing fish.
Disinfect siphons, nets and brushes that touched infected fish. Improve hygiene and lower stocking density.
Use a heater to keep the temperature stable, avoid overstocking and remove bullying fish.
Change water regularly, avoid overcrowding and check the fish daily.
Stopping treatment early lets tomonts in the substrate release new dinospores, and the disease comes back.
Relying on Indian almond leaves does nothing against the parasite.
Low-wattage or fast-flow UV units do not kill dinospores.
In heavily stocked tanks, dinospores can reinfect fish before copper kills them.
Fish with no spots left may still not be cured, because parasites remain in the water and substrate.
Returning treated fish to an untreated main tank can reinfect them.
Vietnamese names for velvet include bệnh nhung, nấm velvet, bệnh gỉ sắt and bệnh bụi vàng.
A Vietnamese guide names Bettazing (12 drops per 4 L) and Maracide as betta remedies for velvet.
The same guide suggests about 1 teaspoon of salt per 10 L as routine prevention, added only at water changes.
A Vietnamese betta blog names Coppersafe and Aquarisol as copper drugs, and Aquatronics Clear Ich for fish sensitive to malachite green.
One Vietnamese betta blog says to raise water to about 21–26°C, which is unusually low compared with other sources.
A Vietnamese source says goldfish and zebrafish are more prone to velvet.
Vietnamese sources call velvet a fungus (nấm velvet), but it is caused by a parasite, Oodinium.
BW Aquatics says salt has little effect on velvet. The benefit of heat-plus-salt comes from the heat, and salt only helps against secondary infections.
BW Aquatics says covering the tank to starve the parasite does not work, because dinospores survive without a host while light is present.
Aquarium Co-op and Wikipedia instead say the parasite needs light, and recommend 7 days of darkness as a helpful supplement.
Wild bettas tolerate the mid-80s °F for a while, and Betta splendens prefer it.
